q: What is the main difference between the chapter's two kinds of loop?
options: A condition loop runs its block once, a counted loop runs it twice
A counted loop works only on text, a condition loop only on numbers
A condition loop repeats while an expression is true, a counted loop runs once per item of a sequence
A condition loop always stops after ten passes, a counted loop never stops
why: Some loops repeat while a condition holds, others run once for each item of a sequence.

q: Why can you not always tell in advance how many times a condition loop will run?
options: Python picks the number of passes at random each time
It stops when its expression turns false, which depends on the data the program meets
A condition loop always runs at least one hundred passes
The block of such a loop is not allowed to change any variable
why: A condition loop repeats as long as an expression is true, so its length depends on the data rather than on a count.

q: What does this program print?
why: The loop keeps going while n is not 1, so the number of passes depends on the data: 6, 3, 10, 5, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1 takes eight steps.

q: How does a while statement differ from an if statement with the same condition?
options: The block of a while statement can never contain an if statement
After the block, execution jumps back and the condition is tested again
A while statement tests its condition only once, before the first pass
An if statement repeats its block, a while statement runs it once
why: Unlike an if statement, a while statement jumps back to the start of its block and tests the condition again after every pass.

q: What does this program print?
code:
total = 0
n = 1
while total < 10:
    total += n
    n += 1
print(total, n)
why: The condition is tested after every pass: total goes 1, 3, 6, 10 and the loop stops as soon as total is no longer below 10, with n having been raised to 5.

q: Which of these can end a deliberate while True: loop?
options: Only break, since nothing else can leave the loop
break, return, sys.exit() or an exception
The condition becoming false after enough passes
Python stops it by itself after about a thousand passes
why: A loop whose condition never becomes false runs until something inside it leaves: break, return, sys.exit() or an exception.

q: What does this program print?
why: while True: never ends by its condition, so only the break inside leaves the loop, and it fires on the first pass where n exceeds 10, which is n = 12.

q: A loop starts with while count < 5: and its block prints count but never changes it. What is the problem?
options: Python refuses to run a while loop whose block has no assignment
The condition can never become false, so nothing inside ever leaves the loop
The loop runs exactly five times because the limit is 5
The loop runs zero times, because count is not compared with anything
why: If the condition never becomes false the program keeps going forever, unless something inside leaves the loop.

q: Why is the length of a counted loop known before it starts?
options: Python counts the passes of the last run and repeats that number
The programmer must always write the number of passes inside the block
It stops when an expression turns false, so the count is fixed by the data
It runs once for each item of a sequence that already exists
why: A counted loop runs its block once for each item of a sequence, so its length is known before it starts.

q: What does this program print?
code:
words = ['a', 'bb', 'ccc']
count = 0
for w in words:
    count += len(w)
print(count)
options: abccc
why: The loop takes each of the three words in turn and adds its length, 1 + 2 + 3.

q: What does a for statement do with the iterable it is given?
options: Takes each item in turn, assigns it to its variable and runs the block once for each
Copies the whole iterable into the variable and runs the block once
Runs the block once and then tests a condition again
Sorts the items first and then runs the block on the largest
why: A for statement takes each item of an iterable in turn, assigns it to its variable and runs the block once for each.

q: What does this program print?
code:
total = 0
for i in range(1, 5):
    total += i * i
print(total)
why: range(1, 5) gives 1, 2, 3, 4 and the block adds their squares: 1 + 4 + 9 + 16.

q: What is range() for in the chapter's loops?
options: It repeats a block a fixed number of times without any loop
It converts a list of numbers into text
It checks whether a number lies between two limits
It makes a sequence of integers for a loop to go through
why: Loops need something to iterate over, and range() is the chapter's way of making a sequence of integers.

q: How many arguments can the range function take?
options: Exactly one, the stop value
Exactly two, start and stop
One, two or three
Any number, which it adds up
why: The range function makes an arithmetic progression of integers and takes one, two or three arguments.

q: Why does list(range(5)) not contain 5?
options: The counting starts at 0 and stops before the argument
range(5) starts at 1, so it holds 1 to 4
The last value is dropped whenever the list is printed
Python leaves out the value that equals the argument to save one step
why: With one argument range starts at 0 and the end point is never part of the sequence.

q: What does this program print?
code: print(len(range(7)), max(range(7)), sum(range(4)))
why: range(7) holds seven values 0 to 6, so its length is 7 and its largest value 6; range(4) holds 0, 1, 2, 3 which add up to 6.

q: A student wants the numbers 1 to 10 and writes range(1, 10). What is wrong?
options: The stop value is excluded, so it ends at 9 and range(1, 11) is needed
Nothing, because range includes both ends
It starts at 0 instead of 1
It gives ten numbers but in descending order
why: The end point of range is never part of the sequence, so range(1, 10) stops at 9.

q: Which call gives the same values as range(10)?
options: range(1, 10)
range(1, 11)
range(0, 9)
why: range(10), range(0, 10) and range(0, 10, 1) all give the same values, from 0 up to but not including 10.

q: What does this program print?
code: print(list(range(2, 6)) == list(range(2, 6, 1)), len(range(12, 16)), list(range(4, 4)))
options: True 5 []
False 4 []
True 4 []
True 4 [4]
why: The default step is 1, so both lists match; range(12, 16) holds 12 to 15, four values; and range(4, 4) begins where it must stop, so it is empty.

q: What does the third argument of range() do?
options: It sets how many values the range holds in total
It sets the value where the range stops
It sets the gap between one value and the next
It repeats every value that many times
why: A third argument is the step between values.

q: What does this program print?
code: print(list(range(1, 10, 3)), list(range(0, 10, 5)))
why: Each value is the previous plus the step, and the stop value is never reached or included: 10 and 10 are excluded.

q: Why does list(range(5, -1, -1)) end with 0 rather than -1?
options: The stop value is still excluded, even when counting down
The negative step turns -1 into 0
Python never produces negative numbers in a range
The stop value is included only when the step is negative
why: A negative step counts down, and the stop value is still excluded.

q: What does this program print?
code: print(list(range(10, 0, -3)), list(range(3, 5, -1)))
why: Counting down by 3 from 10 gives 10, 7, 4, 1 and the next value would pass the stop 0; range(3, 5, -1) starts below its stop while going down, so it is empty.

q: Why does range(1000000) not use much memory?
options: It keeps only the first ten values and guesses the rest
Python compresses the numbers into a text string
It is a list, but a list of small numbers takes little space
It produces its values when iterated instead of holding them in a list
why: A range is an object that produces its values when iterated, not a list holding them, which saves space.

q: What does this program print?
code:
r = range(3)
print(r, list(r), type(r).__name__)
options: range(0, 3) [0, 1, 2] range
range(3) [0, 1, 2] range
range(0, 3) range(0, 3) range
why: Printing a range shows range(0, 3), not the numbers; the numbers appear only when it is iterated, for example by list(), and its type is range.

q: Which job does each of enumerate and zip take over from index arithmetic?
options: enumerate walks several sequences together, zip adds a running count
Both add a count, but zip counts from the end
enumerate sorts the items, zip joins them into one string
enumerate adds a running count to the items, zip walks several sequences together
why: Two built-in functions replace most index arithmetic: one adds a count, the other walks several sequences together.

q: Why is enumerate preferred to range(len(a)) when both the position and the item are needed?
options: It is the only way Python allows to read a list item
It runs faster because it skips the first item
It hands out the position and the item together, with no index arithmetic
It returns only the positions, so the items must be read separately
why: enumerate pairs each item with a running count, replacing range(len(a)) when both are needed.

q: What does this program print?
options: tac
tic toe
tic tac toe
0 tic 2 toe
why: enumerate pairs each name with a count starting at 0, and the if keeps only the pairs whose count is even: positions 0 and 2.

q: What does zip do with sequences of different lengths, and what changes with strict=True?
options: It stops at the shortest by default, and strict=True raises ValueError instead
It pads the short ones with None by default, and strict=True removes the padding
It raises ValueError by default, and strict=True makes it stop at the shortest
It stops at the longest by default, and strict=True stops at the shortest
why: zip stops at the shortest by default; strict=True raises ValueError when the lengths differ instead of truncating silently.

q: What does this program print?
code:
pairs = list(zip('abc', [1, 2]))
try:
    list(zip('abc', [1, 2], strict=True))
    status = 'ok'
except ValueError:
    status = 'ValueError'
print(len(pairs), status)
options: 3 ValueError
2 ok
2 ValueError
3 ok
why: The plain zip stops at the shorter list and gives two pairs, while the strict version sees the lengths differ and raises ValueError.

q: Which pairing of a loop-control tool with its effect is correct?
options: break leaves the loop, continue skips to the next pass
break skips to the next pass, continue leaves the loop
continue ends the whole program, break ends one pass
break and continue both restart the loop from the first item
why: break ends the loop at once while continue skips the rest of the block and goes on with the loop.

q: What is an early exit from a loop?
options: A loop whose body runs zero times
Leaving the loop, or the whole program, before the loop's own test would end it
Skipping one pass and carrying on with the next
A loop that stops because its sequence ran out of items
why: Some programs must leave a loop, or the whole program, before the loop's own test would.

q: When loops are nested, which loop does break end?
options: All the enclosing loops at once
The outermost loop
Only the loop that has an else clause
The innermost enclosing loop
why: break ends the innermost enclosing for or while loop at once.

q: What does this program print?
options: 0 0; end
why: break ends only the inner loop, so each pass of the outer loop prints one pair with b equal to 0 and then the outer loop goes on.

q: What does this program print?
options: else 2
else 1
why: break ends the loop at once and skips its else clause, and the loop variable keeps the value it had when the loop was left.

q: Which exception does sys.exit() raise?
options: KeyboardInterrupt
RuntimeError
ExitError
SystemExit
why: sys.exit() raises SystemExit, which ends the program unless something intercepts it.

q: What does this program print?
options: caught 3 after
after
caught 3
caught None after
why: sys.exit(3) only raises SystemExit, so an except clause can catch it, and the program goes on after the try statement; the exception carries the argument 3.

q: How does skipping a pass differ from leaving a loop?
options: Skipping ends the loop, leaving goes on with the next pass
Skipping goes on with the next pass, leaving ends the loop
Skipping ends the program, leaving ends only the loop
They are the same, only the keyword differs
why: Skipping a pass is different from leaving the loop: the loop continues.

q: In a while loop, where does execution go after continue?
options: Back to test the loop's condition
To the first line after the loop
To the next line of the block
Out of the loop, skipping its else clause
why: continue skips the rest of the block and goes back to test the condition of a while loop.

q: What does this program print?
why: continue skips the adding for 3 and 6, so the total is 1 + 2 + 4 + 5 + 7.

q: In a while loop, why is a continue placed before the line that changes the counter risky?
options: continue ends the loop, so the counter is never used
continue resets the counter to zero
It goes back to the test without changing the counter, so the condition may never change
Python forbids any statement after continue in a block
why: continue skips the rest of the block and goes back to test the condition, so lines after it do not run on that pass.

q: Which pair of facts about a finished loop over a non-empty sequence is true?
options: The else clause runs after every break, and the loop variable is deleted
The loop variable is deleted, and the else clause runs only after an exception
The else clause never runs, and the loop variable is reset to 0
The else clause shows that break was not used, and the loop variable keeps its last value
why: How a loop finishes can be told apart from how it was left, and the loop variable is not deleted when the loop ends.

q: Which task fits the else clause of a for loop best?
options: Run cleanup code even if an exception happens
Run the block a second time if the first pass failed
Report that a search went through everything and found nothing
Run when the loop's sequence is empty and only then
why: The else clause runs when the loop finishes without break, which is the tidy way to say searched everything and found nothing.

q: What does this program print?
options: no even
even 8
even 8 no even
even 3
why: The loop reaches 8, prints and breaks, so the else clause, which runs only when the loop ends without break, is skipped.

q: What does this program print?
options: found found missing
found missing found
found missing missing
missing missing missing
why: A return inside the loop skips the else clause, and a search that finds nothing, including one over an empty list, runs it.

q: After a for loop over a non-empty list ends, what does its loop variable hold?
options: Nothing, because the name is deleted when the loop ends
The value of the last pass, since the name is not deleted
The first item of the list
The number of passes the loop made
why: The loop variable is overwritten on each pass and is not deleted when the loop ends.

q: What does this program print?
why: The for statement overwrites its target on every pass, so changing i inside the block does not change the loop, and after the last pass i still holds what the block last gave it: 2 * 10.

q: What does this program print?
options: None
NameError
why: After a loop over an empty sequence the loop variable was never assigned, so using it raises NameError.

q: What must a program do before it can call a standard library function such as randint?
options: Nothing, all library functions are always available
Copy the function's code into the program
Save the program in the same folder as Python
Import the module that holds the function
why: A program reaches the standard library's functions by importing the module that holds them.

q: How many forms of the import statement does the chapter show?
options: Three: one module, several modules on one line, and a star import
One, since all imports work the same way
Two: import and export
Four, one for each kind of module
why: The chapter shows three forms of the import statement, and PEP 8 has a view on each.

q: After import random, how does a program call the function randint?
options: randint(1, 10), with no prefix
import.randint(1, 10)
random.randint(1, 10), with the module name in front
random(randint, 1, 10)
why: import makes a module's names available under the module's name, as random.randint(1, 10).

q: What does this program print?
options: NameError 2
NameError NameError
2 NameError
why: After a plain import the function is only available under the module's name, so floor alone is unknown, while math.floor(2.7) works.

q: What does import random, sys, os, math do, and what does PEP 8 usually say about it?
options: Imports only random, and PEP 8 prefers this form
Imports all four modules in one statement, and PEP 8 prefers separate lines
Imports all four, and PEP 8 requires this form
Raises SyntaxError, since one import can name only one module
why: One import statement can name several modules separated by commas, but PEP 8 says imports should usually be on separate lines.

q: What does this program print?
code:
import math, string
print(math.ceil(2.1), string.ascii_lowercase[:3])
options: 2 abc
3 a
2 cba
3 abc
why: Both modules are imported by one statement and stay under their own names: math.ceil(2.1) rounds up to 3 and the first three lowercase letters are abc.

q: Why do the chapter and PEP 8 discourage from random import *?
options: It hides which names are present, and the full name reads better
It is slower to run than a plain import
It imports only the first function of the module
It stops working when the module has more than ten names
why: The chapter concludes that the full name makes more readable code, and PEP 8 says wildcard imports make it unclear which names are present.

q: What does this program print?
code:
from math import *
print(sqrt(9), pi > 3)
options: 3 True
3.0 False
3.0 True
NameError
why: from math import * brings sqrt and pi in without the module prefix, so sqrt(9) is the float 3.0 and pi is above 3.

q: A file has two star imports and later calls sqrt(9). What is the reader's problem?
options: The second star import deletes the first one
Python raises an error for a second star import
The call runs twice, once for each module
They cannot tell which module the name sqrt came from
why: Wildcard imports make it unclear which names are present, so the origin of a bare name is hidden.

q: Why does an advanced course add a section beyond the chapter's loops?
options: Because the chapter's loops no longer work in current Python
To replace for and while by newer statements
To pair the loops with what current Python offers and the hazards the documentation names
To teach features that only exist in Python 3.14
why: An advanced course pairs the chapter's loops with what current Python offers for the same jobs, and with the hazards the reference documentation names.

q: Which two features does the expression style group cover?
options: The range function and the enumerate function
The break statement and the continue statement
Star imports and the sys.exit function
The := assignment expression in loop conditions and the PEP 8 advice on imports
why: Two recent language and style features shorten and tidy the loops and imports the chapter teaches.

q: Since which Python version can := name a value inside a condition?
why: Since Python 3.8 an assignment expression names a value inside a condition.

q: What does this program print?
code:
items = iter(['ab', 'cd', '', 'ef'])
got = []
while chunk := next(items):
    got.append(chunk)
print(got, repr(chunk))
options: ['ab', 'cd', 'ef'] 'ef'
['ab', 'cd'] 'cd'
why: The condition names each value as it tests it, so the loop stops at the empty string, which is false, and chunk still holds that value afterwards.

q: What does PEP 8 advise about wildcard imports?
options: Avoid them, with one exception for republishing an internal interface as a public API
Use them whenever a module has many names
Use them only inside functions
Always use them for the standard library
why: PEP 8 advises against wildcard imports, with the single defensible exception of republishing an internal interface as part of a public API.

q: A file needs os, sys and math. Which arrangement follows the PEP 8 advice?
options: One line: import os, sys, math
One line per module, each written as a star import
One star import from a module that holds all three
Three lines, one import statement per module, and no wildcard
why: PEP 8 advises one import per line and against wildcard imports.

q: What do the two hazards in this group have in common?
options: Both are errors that stop the program at once
Both only occur in old versions of Python
Both are caused by using range() the wrong way
Both are traps named in the reference documentation that are easy to write without noticing
why: Two hazards the documentation names are worth teaching beside the chapter's programs.

q: What is the tutorial's remedy for changing a collection while looping over it?
options: Loop over a copy, or build a new collection
Change the collection only inside a continue statement
Sort the collection before the loop
Use while True: so the loop never ends
why: Changing a collection while iterating over it is tricky to get right; the remedy is to loop over a copy or build a new collection.

q: What does this program print?
why: Removing items from the list being looped over shifts the later items so some are never visited, while looping over a copy visits them all.

q: What does this program print?
options: RuntimeError
KeyError
why: Deleting from the dictionary that the loop is walking over is the hazard the tutorial names, and Python stops the loop with an error.

q: What does Python 3.14 do when return, break or continue leaves a finally block?
options: It raises a SyntaxError and refuses to run the file
It says nothing, as in every earlier version
It raises RuntimeError when the statement is reached
The compiler emits a SyntaxWarning
why: Python 3.14 makes the compiler emit a SyntaxWarning when a return, break or continue statement has the effect of leaving a finally block, as PEP 765 specifies.

q: Under Python 3.14, a script has break inside a finally block in a loop. What happens when it is run?
options: The script does not start at all because of a SyntaxError
The compiler warns, and the script still runs
Nothing at all is reported
The break is silently turned into a continue
why: The change adds a SyntaxWarning, which is a warning and not an error, so the code is still compiled and run.

q: Why does the chapter define the words loop and iteration before it introduces while and for?
options: Both words are used throughout the book and the documentation, so later sections can rely on them
Python refuses to run a loop statement in a program that has not defined the word first
Both words are keywords of the language and have to be imported before they are used
They are the names of the two built-in loop statements that the chapter then compares, which is why they are explained so early in the text
why: The two words are used constantly, so they are defined first and the later sections build on them.

q: If the condition is true at first, what is the only difference between an if clause and a while clause?
options: A while clause may hold only one statement, while an if clause may hold as many as you like
An if clause tests its condition twice before it runs, a while clause tests it only one time
A while clause runs only when its condition is false at first, an if clause only when it is true, and that is the reason the two statements are written with different keywords
At the end of the while clause execution jumps back to the start of the statement and the condition is tested again
why: The book compares the two statements and finds that only the jump back to the start of the block separates them.

q: What does the book call the indented block that follows the line of a loop statement?
options: The header of the loop
The index of the loop
The clause of the loop
The condition of the loop
why: A while or for line ends with a colon and is followed by an indented block, which the book calls the loop's clause.

q: What does a loop add to the if statement of chapter 2?
options: It lets a block choose between two alternatives, where an if statement has only one
It decides how often a block runs, where an if statement decides whether the block runs
It lets a block run in the background while the rest of the program goes on without waiting for the block to finish
It lets a block run before the lines that are written above it in the file
why: Both statements guard a block, but a loop sends execution back to its start so that the block can run many times.

q: What is one iteration of a loop?
options: The first line of the loop's block
A single execution of the loop's block
The test that decides whether the loop goes on
The variable that counts how often the loop has run
why: An iteration is one pass through the block, so a loop that runs five times makes five iterations.

q: What does this program print?
code:
count = 0
for i in range(3):
    count += 1
print(count, i)
why: The block runs once for each of the values 0, 1 and 2, so count is 3, and i keeps the last value, 2.

q: Which parts does a while loop need to do the work of for i in range(5)?
options: Only the test i < 5, because a while loop raises i by itself after every pass, so no starting value is required either
A break that fires when i equals 5, and no test at the top of the loop
A call to range(5) placed inside the condition of the while statement
A starting assignment i = 0, the test i < 5 and an increase of i at the end of the block
why: The for statement does the counting for you; in a while loop the starting value, the test and the increase must all be written out.

q: What does this program print?
code:
total = 0
i = 0
while i < 5:
    total += i
    i += 1
print(total)
why: The loop adds 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 and stops when i reaches 5, which gives 10.

q: Why must an accumulator get its starting value before the loop?
options: Python resets every variable to zero at the beginning of each pass of a loop
A for loop refuses to start unless some variable equals zero beforehand
The first update reads the variable, so it has to exist already
The starting value decides how many passes the loop is going to make
why: A statement such as total = total + num needs a total that already exists, otherwise it raises a NameError.

q: What does this program print?
code:
total = 0
for n in range(4):
    total += n * n
print(total)
why: The squares 0, 1, 4 and 9 are added one by one, which makes 14.

q: What does the chapter do with the single loops once they are understood?
options: It combines them into two complete programs, one of which has a loop inside another loop
It replaces them with recursion, which the two programs then use throughout and in every later chapter of the book
It shows that each loop must be written in a separate file of its own
It removes the while loop from the language in favour of the for loop
why: Guess the Number and Rock, Paper, Scissors are built from the loops of the chapter, and the second contains a loop within a loop.

q: How do the loops of the two example programs differ in the way they end?
options: Both programs end their loops through the condition at the top, and neither uses break or sys.exit()
The guessing loop is endless, while the game's main loop runs exactly three times
Both loops end after the same number of passes, which is fixed by the random module, so the player cannot influence when a game ends in either program
The guessing loop makes at most six passes or breaks on a correct guess, while the game's main loop ends only when the player quits
why: Guess the Number counts attempts with range(1, 7) and breaks on success, while the main game loop is while True and ends through sys.exit().

q: What does break do when it runs inside the inner one of two nested loops?
options: It leaves both loops at once and continues after the outer loop
It skips the rest of the current pass of the outer loop only, and the inner loop is started again from its first value
It ends the program in the same way as sys.exit() does
It leaves only the inner loop, and the outer loop goes on with its next pass
why: A break leaves the innermost loop that contains it; to leave both, another means such as sys.exit() is needed.

q: What does this program print?
why: The inner loop runs 0 times for i = 0, once for i = 1 and twice for i = 2, so n becomes 3.

q: Why can the code after the loop still read guess and guesses_taken?
options: Python stores the variables of every loop in a file and reads them back later
Variables assigned by a loop keep their values after the loop has ended
The variables are deleted only when the program is closed by the user
The break statement copies them to the code that follows the loop
why: A loop does not have a scope of its own, so the loop variable and the names assigned in its block remain available.

q: What happens in Guess the Number when the player types abc at the prompt?
options: int() raises a ValueError and the program stops
The text counts as a guess that is too low and the loop goes on
input() asks again until the player types a valid whole number
The break statement runs and the failure message is printed
why: The text returned by input() is passed to int(), which cannot convert abc and raises a ValueError that nothing catches.

q: What is the job of the inner while True loop of Rock, Paper, Scissors?
options: It keeps asking until the player enters a valid move or the quit command
It plays the three rounds of one game before the score is shown, after which the main loop asks whether to continue
It lets the computer pick a new random move after every wrong answer
It repeats the whole game until the score has reached ten points
why: The inner loop is the player input loop: it prints the prompt, reads a move and loops again unless the move is valid or q.

q: Why does the game use sys.exit() for the quit command rather than break?
options: sys.exit() is the only statement that can leave a loop of the form while True
A break cannot be written inside an if statement that sits within a loop
sys.exit() also saves the final score of the player to a file on disk and prints it before the program ends
A break would leave only the inner input loop, and the main game loop would go on
why: The quit command must end the whole program from inside two loops, and a break leaves only the innermost one.

q: Why is a half-open range convenient for ranges that follow each other?
options: The end of each range is counted twice, which makes it easy to see where one ends
Half-open ranges are the only ones that Python allows in a for statement, and that is why the start is always included but the end never is
The end of one range is the start of the next, so range(0, 5) and range(5, 10) fit together without a gap or overlap
The start is left out of such a range, so it can be reused by the previous one
why: Because the end is excluded, the values of range(0, 5) followed by those of range(5, 10) are exactly the values of range(10).

q: What does this program print?
code:
a = list(range(2, 7))
print(len(a), a[-1])
why: The range 2, 7 holds 7 - 2 = 5 numbers, and the last of them is 6 because 7 is excluded.

q: Which operation on a range raises a TypeError?
options: Asking whether a number is in the range
Joining two ranges with +
Taking a slice of the range
Asking for the length of the range
why: A range does not support + because the result would usually not be an arithmetic progression, whereas membership, slices and len work.

q: What does this program print?
code:
r = range(0, 20, 2)
print(r[3], 7 in r, len(r))
options: 6 False 10
3 False 10
6 True 10
6 False 9
why: The range 0, 2, ..., 18 has ten values, its item at position 3 is 6, and 7 is not among its even values.

q: What does the target part i, v of for i, v in enumerate(items) do?
options: It creates a dictionary with the keys i and v in every pass of the loop
It checks that the list called items has exactly two elements
It makes i and v refer to the same value as long as the loop runs
It unpacks each pair that enumerate delivers into the two names i and v
why: Each item of the loop is a tuple of position and element, and the two targets receive its parts.

q: What does this program print?
options: a2b
aab
abb
ab
why: The pairs give 'a' repeated once and 'b' repeated twice, and end='' keeps them on one line.

q: Which two methods form the iterator protocol, according to the library documentation?
options: __len__() and __getitem__()
__enter__() and __exit__()
__iter__() and __next__()
__init__() and __call__()
why: One method returns the iterator and the other delivers the next item, raising StopIteration when there are none.

q: What happens when a for loop asks an exhausted iterator for another item?
options: The iterator starts again from its first item and the loop goes on
StopIteration is raised, and the for loop ends quietly
A ValueError is raised and the program stops with a traceback
The loop receives None and runs its block once more
why: The for statement calls next() behind the scenes and treats StopIteration as the signal that the sequence has run out.

q: Why does for i in 5 fail?
options: An integer is not iterable, so no iterator can be made from it
The variable i has not been assigned before the loop starts
The number 5 is too small to be used as a loop sequence, since a for loop needs at least ten items
A for loop is allowed only inside a function definition
why: Calling iter(5) raises a TypeError, which is what the loop does first; range(5) is what supplies five values.

q: What does this program print?
code:
d = {'x': 1, 'y': 2}
print(list(d))
why: Walking through a dictionary visits its keys, so list(d) is the list of keys.

q: How does an iterator differ from the iterable it was made from?
options: It stores all of its items in a list that can be read as often as you like and can be restarted at any time
It can be indexed with square brackets in the same way as a string
It is a copy of the iterable that can be changed without affecting the original
It delivers the items one at a time and is used up once they have all been delivered
why: An iterable can produce iterators; each iterator remembers its position and cannot go back.

q: What does this program print?
code:
it = iter([1, 2, 3])
next(it)
print(list(it))
why: The call next(it) consumes the first item, so list(it) holds only what remains.

q: Why does a chapter on loops introduce lists, tuples and dictionaries?
options: Python allows a for loop to run over these three types and no others, so they have to be taught before the loops
Loops are written to process collections, and the examples use them from the start
The three types are the only ones that can be compared with an if statement
Each of the three types has its own loop statement in the language
why: The chapter's loops walk through collections, so the three types are explained only as far as the chapter uses them.

q: Which of the three collection types is looked up by arbitrary keys instead of positions?
options: The dictionary
The tuple
The list
The range
why: A dictionary maps keys to values, whereas lists, tuples and ranges are indexed by integer positions.

q: Why does the glossary class a dictionary as a mapping and not as a sequence?
options: Its lookups use arbitrary hashable keys, not integer positions
It cannot be used in a for loop, which accepts only sequences
It has no length, so len() cannot be applied to it
Its items cannot be changed after the dictionary has been created
why: A sequence is accessed by integer indices and has a length; a dictionary has a length too, but its lookups use keys.

q: What does this program print?
code:
s = 'python'
print(s[1], s[-1], len(s))
options: p n 6
y n 5
y o 6
y n 6
why: Position 1 of 'python' is 'y', position -1 counts from the end and is 'n', and the length is 6.

q: Why is a list the right choice when a collection has to change?
options: It is the only collection that a for loop is able to walk through, which is why the chapter's loops use it
It keeps its items in sorted order whenever one of them changes
Its items can be replaced and added in place, which strings and tuples do not allow
It stores each item only once, which saves memory in long loops
why: Assigning to an item of a string or tuple raises a TypeError, while a list accepts a[0] = 99 and append.

q: What does this program print?
code:
a = [1, 2]
b = a
b.append(3)
print(a)
why: The names a and b refer to the same list, so the item appended through b is seen through a.

q: Which statement about ('hello') and ('hello',) is correct?
options: Both are tuples, and the comma only changes how they are printed
The first is just a string, and the second is a tuple of length 1
The first is a tuple of five characters and the second a tuple of length 1
Both are strings, because parentheses never make a tuple
why: It is the comma that makes a tuple, so ('hello',) has one item and ('hello') is the string in parentheses.

q: What does this program print?
code:
t = (5, 6)
a, b = t
print(b, a, len(t))
why: The assignment unpacks the pair into a = 5 and b = 6, and the tuple still has length 2.

q: What happens when a dictionary is asked for a key that does not exist?
options: None is returned and the program goes on
The key is added with the value 0
An IndexError is raised with the position of the key
A KeyError is raised
why: Looking up a missing key with square brackets raises KeyError, for example KeyError: 'Eda'.

q: What does this program print?
code:
users = {'Ada': 'active', 'Can': 'inactive'}
print(len(users), users['Can'])
options: 2 active
1 inactive
2 inactive
3 inactive
why: The dictionary has two pairs, and the lookup users['Can'] gives 'inactive'.

q: Which key combination interrupts a running Python program in a terminal?
options: Control-V
Control-P
Control-C
Control-W
why: Control-C makes Python raise KeyboardInterrupt in the running code.

q: What does this program print?
options: KeyboardInterrupt
stopped
Hello, world!
(no output)
why: The exception raised inside the loop is caught by the handler, which prints stopped, and the program ends normally.

q: Why can a return statement end a loop?
options: It leaves the whole function, so the loop ends with it and its else clause does not run
It jumps to the next pass of the loop and keeps the function running, skipping the rest of the block of the current pass
It stops only the loop and continues with the next line of the function
It is allowed in a loop only when the loop is the last statement of the program
why: A return ends the function that contains the loop, so nothing after it in the function runs.

q: What does this program print?
options: 4 None
None None
3 None
why: The first call returns 3, the first item above 2, and the second call finds none and reaches return None.

q: In which case does the else clause of a loop run?
options: When the loop is left through a break statement
Whenever the block of the loop has raised an exception
Only when the loop made no pass at all
When the loop ends because its condition becomes false or its sequence runs out
why: The else clause belongs to normal completion; break, return and an uncaught exception all skip it.

q: What does this program print?
why: After the first pass n is 4, after the second it is 8, which is above 5, so break leaves the loop and the else clause is skipped.

q: How does a warning differ from an exception?
options: A warning stops the program at once, while an exception is only written to a log, and nothing else distinguishes the two in practice
A warning reports something suspicious and lets the program go on, while an exception interrupts the normal flow
A warning can be raised only by the user, while an exception comes from Python
A warning is printed to the screen, while an exception is never shown to the user
why: Exceptions change the flow of the program unless they are handled; warnings only report.

q: Why does except Exception not catch KeyboardInterrupt or SystemExit?
options: They derive from BaseException and not from Exception
They are warnings and not exceptions, so a handler cannot see them
They are raised only outside of loops, where no handler applies
They are subclasses of ValueError and are handled by a separate clause
why: The documentation derives these two directly from BaseException so that a handler for Exception does not swallow a request to stop.

q: What does the last line of an uncaught error message tell you?
options: The type of the exception and its details
The line of the program that will run next
The name of the user who started the program
The number of seconds the program ran before it failed
why: The traceback shows where the exception occurred, and its last line gives the type and the details, such as ZeroDivisionError: division by zero.

q: What does this program print?
options: x
ValueError
(no output)
why: int('x') raises a ValueError, the handler assigns 0, and the program goes on to print it.

q: When does the finally clause of a try statement run?
options: Only when the try block has raised an exception that no except clause has handled before it
Only when the try block ended without any exception
On every way out of the try block, including an exception, a break or a return
Only when the program is closed by the user
why: The clause is for clean-up that must happen whatever happened, so it runs on the way out however the block is left.

q: What does this program print?
options: f1
ff1
fff2
ff2
why: The finally clause prints f in the pass for i = 0 and again on the way out of the break at i = 1, and then i is 1.

q: What does Python 3.14 do when a break statement leaves a finally block?
options: It raises a SyntaxError and refuses to run the program, so that the mistake is found before any output appears
It compiles the code and issues a SyntaxWarning, and the program still runs
It ignores the break and says nothing at all
It changes the break into a return without telling anyone
why: The check is a warning and not an error, so existing programs keep running.

q: Why does the same code produce no warning under Python 3.12?
options: The check was added to the compiler only in Python 3.14
Python 3.12 does not allow a finally block inside a loop
The warning is shown only when the program is run in a terminal
Python 3.12 turns every warning off unless a flag is given
why: The behaviour of the code is unchanged between the versions; only the 3.14 compiler reports it.

q: After from math import sqrt, which statement is correct?
options: math.sqrt(16) works, and sqrt(16) raises a NameError
Both sqrt(16) and math.sqrt(16) work
Neither works, because only import math makes the functions available
sqrt(16) works without the prefix, and the name math does not exist
why: The from form copies the listed names into the program and does not bind the module's own name.

q: What does this program print?
code:
from math import sqrt
print(sqrt(49))
options: NameError
why: sqrt returns a float, so the square root of 49 is printed as 7.0.

q: Which statement about a module is correct?
options: A module is a loop that Python runs once for each name in a program and that ends with the last name of the program
A module is a variable that holds the result of the last import
A module is a file of Python code, and its names are reached through the module's own namespace
A module is a function that is always available in a fresh program
why: The glossary calls a module an organizational unit of Python code that has a namespace of its own.

q: A fresh program calls math.sqrt(16) without importing math. What happens?
options: An ImportError is raised, because the module cannot be found on the search path of the interpreter
A NameError is raised, because the name math does not exist yet
The call works, because math is a built-in name
An AttributeError is raised, because sqrt is not defined
why: Until import math has run, the name math is not defined in the program.

q: What is the name of the module that a file called fibo.py defines?
options: fibo
fibo.py
__main__
module
why: The file name is the module name with the suffix .py appended, and the module's name is held in __name__.

q: What is the value of __name__ in a file that is run directly as the program?
options: The name of the file
'module'
None
'__main__'
why: A module that is imported has its own name, while the file that is run directly gets the name '__main__'.

q: Why does len('hello') work in a fresh program while math.sqrt(16) does not?
options: len belongs to the standard library, but math is not part of it, so it must be installed separately with pip
math.sqrt needs a newer version of Python than len does
len is imported automatically, while sqrt is a keyword
len is a built-in function, while math is a module that has to be imported first
why: Built-in functions are available at once; the other modules of the standard library are loaded by an import statement.

q: What does the standard library consist of?
options: Programs that every student has to write before the course starts
Packages that must be downloaded from the internet before use with a package manager such as pip, in the same way as other packages
Modules that come with Python, each holding a related group of functions
The built-in keywords of the language, such as while and for
why: The standard library ships with Python as a collection of modules.

q: What does a separate namespace for each module prevent?
options: A module from reading its own variables
Two modules using the same name for different things from clashing
The program from calling a function twice with the same arguments and getting the same answer
A name from being used before it is assigned in the same module
why: Namespaces support modularity by preventing naming conflicts and make clear which module implements a function.

q: What does this program print?
code:
import math
print('sqrt' in dir(math), hasattr(math, 'nope'))
options: True False
True True
False False
False True
why: dir lists the names of the module, so 'sqrt' is among them, and math has no attribute called nope.

q: Which directory is the first entry of sys.path when a script is run?
options: The directory that contains the script
The directory of the standard library
The home directory of the user
The directory where Python was installed, where the standard library is also kept
why: The script's own directory comes first, which is why a local file can hide a standard module.

q: Why is a change in a module's file not noticed by a running session?
options: Python reads module files only when a computer is restarted
Module files are locked while the interpreter is running
The change is noticed only if the file is saved in another folder
A module is imported only once per session and is then found in sys.modules
why: Later imports reuse the loaded module unless it is reloaded with importlib.reload() or the interpreter is restarted.

q: A program saved as random.py is in the same folder as a second program that runs import random. What happens?
options: Python imports the standard module and ignores the file in the folder
Python raises a SyntaxError in the file called random.py as soon as it is found on the search path
The second program imports your file instead of the standard module, so random.randint is missing
Both modules are imported and their names are merged
why: The script's directory comes first on the search path, so the local file is found before the standard library.

q: What does Python 3.14 add to the AttributeError of a clashing file name?
options: A line that deletes the file with the clashing name and then imports the standard module in its place
A hint that suggests renaming the file because it has the same name as a standard library module
A list of all the modules that the program imports
Nothing, because the message is the same in all versions
why: The extra hint appears in 3.14 and is absent in 3.12, which the chapter's checks confirm.

q: Which values can random.randint(1, 3) return?
options: 1 and 2 only, because the end is excluded
1, 2 and 3, because both ends are included
2 only, because the ends are excluded
Any decimal number between 1 and 3, because randint works with floating-point numbers
why: randint(a, b) is an alias for randrange(a, b+1), so b can be returned.

q: What does this program print?
code:
import random
random.seed(5)
a = random.randint(1, 6)
random.seed(5)
b = random.randint(1, 6)
print(a == b)
options: True
False
a
(no output)
why: Seeding with the same value gives the same sequence again, so the two draws are equal.

q: Why does the chapter treat random and sys as the standard modules it needs?
options: They are the only two modules in the standard library that Python allows
Every program has to import both before it can print anything
They are the two modules that replace the loop statements
The two programs of the chapter draw random numbers and end through sys.exit()
why: Guess the Number and Rock, Paper, Scissors use random.randint() and sys.exit(), so these are the library parts the chapter explains.

q: What does this program end with?
code:
import random
print(randint(1, 6))
options: ImportError
TypeError
NameError
AttributeError
why: After a plain import only the module's name exists, so randint alone is an undefined name and the call has to be written random.randint(1, 6).

q: Which name in the sys module lists the directories that are searched for modules?
options: sys.modules
sys.exit
sys.path
sys.argv
why: sys.path is the search path, while sys.modules holds the modules already loaded.

q: What does sys.modules hold?
options: The names of all the modules that exist in the standard library, whether or not the program has used them
The modules that have already been loaded in the running interpreter
The directories that are searched for modules
The functions of the sys module that are still unused
why: After import math the key 'math' is present in sys.modules.
